content: Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) is a common cause of diarrhea, which is typically self-limiting. However, in some cases, it can lead to more severe complications such as sepsis and dehydration. The routine use of antibiotics for NTS infections may contribute to persistent bacterial colonization and the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of administering antibiotics to individuals with NTS-related diarrhea. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they compared antibiotic treatment to placebo or no treatment in symptomatic individuals of all ages. Symptoms considered included fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. Trials that did not report outcomes specifically for the NTS subgroup were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The primary outcome was the presence of diarrhea between two to four days after treatment. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology. A total of 12 trials involving 767 participants were included in the analysis. No significant differences were observed between the antibiotic and placebo/no treatment groups in terms of diarrhea resolution at two to four days after treatment (risk ratio [RR] 1.75, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.42 to 7.21; one trial, 46 participants; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, no differences were found for diarrhea resolution at five to seven days after treatment (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.12; two trials, 192 participants; very low-quality evidence) or for clinical failure (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.25; seven trials, 440 participants; very low-quality evidence). The mean difference in the duration of diarrhea was 0 days (95% CI -0.54 to 0.54; 202 participants, four studies; low-quality evidence). For fever, the mean difference was 0.27 days (95% CI -0.11 to 0.65; 107 participants, two studies; very low-quality evidence). The duration of illness also showed no difference, with a mean difference of 0 days (95% CI -0.68 to 0.68; 116 participants, two studies; very low-quality evidence). Quinolone antibiotics were associated with a significantly higher rate of negative stool cultures for NTS during the first week of treatment (microbiological failure: RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.56; 166 participants, four trials). However, individuals treated with antibiotics were almost twice as likely to shed the same Salmonella serovar in their stool one month after treatment (RR 1.96, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.98; 112 participants, three trials), a statistically significant finding. Non-severe adverse drug reactions were more frequently reported among patients receiving antibiotic treatment. In conclusion, there is no evidence to support the routine use of antibiotics for NTS-related diarrhea in otherwise healthy individuals. The effects of antibiotics in very young children, elderly individuals, and those with severe or extraintestinal disease remain uncertain. A slightly higher incidence of adverse events was observed in patients treated with antibiotics for NTS.
